prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the geometry of a multi-tiered shelving rack with long horizontal boards above a tiled floor, showing the foreground board in frames 1 and 2 at roughly 0.4–0.8 m from the camera wearer (within arm's reach) and receding diagonally to the left toward a second person standing about 1.5–2.0 m away. In frames 2 and 3, the second person's apron-clad lower body and feet are visible on the far left edge, partially cropped out of view and occluded by the rack tiers, facing sideways/toward the rack rather than looking at the camera wearer while holding the far end of the upper board within their arm's reach. Across frames 3 to 5, as the camera wearer turns and tilts their head downward toward the lower shelves, the upper shelf edge remains very bright (about 0.3–0.5 m away, upper right) while the lower shelf (about 0.6–0.9 m below and in front) is grasped by the camera wearer's extended left hand at roughly 0.5 m in frame 4 before being pulled closer in frame 5. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the overlapping spatial planes of the stacked shelves, the protruding cloth edge in frame 2, and the foreground arm in frame 4 from the background floor. However, the depth map is unreliable in dark shadow regions under the shelves and along the far-left floor in frames 3 and 4, where the floor and lower rack structure merge into uniform black.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map attempts to parse the objects in the multi-tiered rack scene, where the camera wearer stands within arm's reach (0.4–0.8 m) of horizontal dough boards while a second person stands about 1.5–2.0 m away to the left in frames 2 and 3, partially out of frame and facing the rack without looking toward the camera wearer. In frame 1, the map masks the foreground cloth-covered board (spanning roughly 0.4–1.5 m in front of the wearer) and parts of the shelf above it, highlighting the contiguous surface extent of the foreground layers relative to the unmasked gap on the right and the dark shelf underside. Beyond isolating that initial foreground surface contour in frame 1, the segmentation map provides almost no spatial information that is hard to see in RGB and is severely unreliable across the sequence. It misclassifies the bakery board and upper shelf in frame 1 as a 'bed' with jagged holes in the mask, and fails completely in frames 2 through 5 by outputting entirely blank black frames. As a result, it misses the tiered shelves, the tiled floor below, the second person on the left in frames 2–3, and the camera wearer's blue-gloved left hand reaching out at 0.5 m to pull the lower board in frames 4–5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is meant to track body and hand skeletons in the workspace as the camera wearer shifts view from the upper board (0.4–1.5 m in front) downward to the lower rack tiers (0.5–1.0 m in front and below) and reaches out with their left hand in frame 4. In frame 2, a single isolated yellow keypoint dot appears near the bottom-left corner, corresponding to the lower leg/ankle of the second person standing roughly 1.5–2.0 m away on the left edge of the frame, about 1.0–1.5 m beyond the foreground cloth edge. While that single dot pinpoints the approximate image location of the partially occluded person's lower limb in frame 2, the pose map otherwise fails to provide any structural skeleton information beyond the RGB view. It is highly unreliable across all five frames because heavy cropping and occlusion by the protruding boards prevent full body detection of the second person (whose torso and head are out of view in frames 2 and 3, facing the rack rather than the camera wearer). Furthermore, it completely fails to detect the camera wearer's own blue-gloved left hand and forearm entering from the bottom center-left within arm's reach (roughly 0.5 m away) to grasp the lower shelf edge in frame 4.
